newsitem.title: INDIA: India may partly sink oil debt in fiscal deficit.
newsitem.headline: India may partly sink oil debt in fiscal deficit.

text.p: A $5.3 billion oil stain over India's national accounts may be partially absorbed into the government's fiscal deficit, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Monday.
This was one option under consideration, along with increases in domestic oil prices, for dealing with a multi-billion dollar debt to oil companies, he said.
The companies are owed the money for selling petroleum products below market prices to support India's subsidy regime.
The oil pool deficit is about 190 billion rupees, up from 155 billion at the start of the financial year on April 1.

The official said petroleum product price increases could be implemented to neutralise the 1997/98 incremental increase in the oil pool deficit, while government support through the fiscal deficit could be used to reduce the stock of debt from previous years.
Up to around 100 billion rupees of old debt could be liquidated over one or two years, he said, stressing that there were no hard proposals.

Press Trust of India earlier reported Finance Ministry sources said consolidating the oil pool account, currently managed by India's Oil Coordination Committee and kept off the government's books, would not push the fiscal deficit above 5.2 percent of gross domestic product.
That means kissing goodbye the 1997/98 (April-March) budget target for a deficit of 4.5 percent of GDP, but the ministry sources said the extra burden was manageable, PTI said.
The oil pool deficit is the stickiest and most pressing economic problem facing Prime Minister Inder Gujral's government.
The mess is a result of India leaving its domestic prices unchanged when world oil prices surged late last year.
The United Front coalition government's policy-making steering committee has failed in its last two meetings to solve the oil riddle, and a third meeting has been deferred several times already.
Sources in New Delhi said the government could announce measures in August, but the timing remained unclear as Gujral's coalition is wrought with internal divisions that could divert its energies.

But the oil companies need money back fast to pay for crude oil supplies needed to keep their refineries working. They are already heavily indebted and are keeping supplies flowing on a hand-to-mouth basis, and lack funds for vital capital investment.
A committee charged with seeking ways to restructure the oil sector's finances suggested the oil debt could be paid for by issuing "petro-bonds".
Sources in New Delhi said the government could announce measures in August, but the timing remained unclear as Gujral's fragile coalition lurched into more trouble on Monday.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, a southern regional party, announced it was planning to leave the government but support it from outside, in protest against the behaviour of some unidentified coalition partners.
The latest squabble does not bode well for convening the coalition's policy-making steering committee.
